aiheet.nimi: The quantum-mechanical model of the atom

kortit.maaritelma: The smallest amount in which a physical quantity can be transferred in an interaction.
In some phenomena energy can be gained or transferred only in definite portions.
The energy quantum of the electromagnetic radiation field; it has no rest mass.
A fundamental constant of quantum physics that links the energy of a photon to the frequency of the radiation.
Grows as the frequency of the radiation grows and its wavelength shrinks.
kortit.kaava_puhe: E is h times f, which is h c divided by lambda

kortit.maaritelma: The energy that a charge with the magnitude of the elementary charge gains when it moves through a potential difference of one volt.
kortit.kaava_puhe: one electronvolt is about 1.60 times 10 to the power minus 19 joules

kortit.maaritelma: An ideal emitter whose radiation spectrum depends only on its temperature.
Contains an unbroken range of wavelengths with no separate spectral lines.
Electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency can release electrons from the surface of a material.
The smallest energy needed to release an electron from the surface of a given material.
The lowest frequency of radiation at which electrons can be released from a given material.
The voltage at which even the fastest electrons released from the surface are just stopped.
The energy of the fastest released electron follows from conservation of energy.
kortit.kaava_puhe: E k max is h f minus W

kortit.maaritelma: The energy of the photon is used for the work function and the kinetic energy of the electron.
kortit.kaava_puhe: h f is W plus E k max

kortit.maaritelma: Tells the radiation energy arriving at a surface per unit area and unit time.
Radiation and matter particles can have both wave-like and particle-like properties.
A massless quantum of radiation has momentum.
kortit.kaava_puhe: p is h divided by lambda, which is E divided by c

kortit.maaritelma: A collision of a photon with an electron changes the energy and wavelength of the photon.
Single particles gradually build up an interference pattern that is characteristic of waves.
A wave-like property associated with a moving matter particle.
The wavelength of a particle depends on its momentum.
kortit.kaava_puhe: lambda is h divided by p

kortit.maaritelma: The combining of waves strengthens or weakens the observed effect at different places.
The short wavelength of electrons makes imaging possible in more detail than with visible light.
An electron in an atom can have only certain allowed energies.
The lowest possible energy state of an atom.
A state of an atom in which its electron system has more energy than in the ground state.
An atom receives energy and moves to a higher energy level.
An atom gives away energy as a photon when it moves to a lower energy level.
An atom receives a photon of suitable energy and moves to a higher energy level.
Contains the wavelengths that excited matter emits when its atoms de-excite to lower energy levels.
Contains the missing wavelengths that matter has absorbed from a continuous spectrum.
Consists of separate wavelengths and tells about the quantised energy states of matter.
Shows the allowed energies of a system and the transitions between them.
The smallest energy needed to release an electron completely from an atom in its ground state.
The allowed energy of the electron depends on the principal quantum number.
kortit.kaava_puhe: E n is minus 13.6 electronvolts divided by n squared

kortit.maaritelma: An allowed state of a system with certain physical properties and an energy.
A mathematical description from which the probabilities of detecting a particle can be determined.
Describes how likely it is that a particle is detected in different regions.
The quantum state of an electron in an atom. In pictures it is drawn as the region where the electron is detected with high probability.
A number that describes the properties of the quantum state of an electron in an atom.
A group of electron states with the same principal quantum number.
In an atom two electrons cannot have all their quantum numbers the same.
The position and the momentum of a particle cannot be determined at the same time with arbitrary accuracy.
According to quantum mechanics a particle can be found on the other side of a barrier without having enough energy in the classical sense.
A wave whose pattern stays in place; the allowed states of a bound electron are standing waves, so only certain quantum states are possible.
A material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled, for example by doping or by changing the temperature.
A small amount of other atoms is added to a semiconductor to change its electrical conductivity.
A semiconductor component that conducts electric current mainly in one direction.
A semiconductor component that can control or amplify an electric current.
A semiconductor device that converts the energy of electromagnetic radiation into electrical energy.
The production of light in matter without strong heating of the matter.
After energy is absorbed, light is produced quickly as the excited state de-excites.
The excited state de-excites slowly, so the material can emit light even after the excitation has ended.
A photon causes an excited atom to emit a second photon of the same energy.
Produces directional, nearly monochromatic and coherent electromagnetic radiation.
The waves oscillate with a constant phase difference between them.
Short-wavelength, high-energy ionising electromagnetic radiation.
Electrons are accelerated by a high voltage and made to hit the anode to produce radiation.
The electrode of an X-ray tube from which electrons are released and accelerated towards the anode.
The target of an X-ray tube that the electrons moving at high speed hit.
Produced when electrons slow down in the electric field of atomic nuclei; it forms the continuous X-ray spectrum.
Produced when an electron of an anode atom drops into a vacancy in an inner shell; it forms spectral lines characteristic of the material.
Consists of continuous bremsstrahlung with characteristic lines on top of it.
The photon of highest energy from an X-ray tube is produced when all the energy of an electron changes into a photon.
kortit.kaava_puhe: lambda min is h c divided by the product e U

kortit.maaritelma: A common name for the protons and neutrons of an atomic nucleus.
A positively charged nucleon whose number determines the element.
An electrically neutral nucleon whose number can vary between nuclei of the same element.
The number of protons in an atomic nucleus.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
Nuclei of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
The unit of mass for atoms and nuclei.
kortit.kaava_puhe: one atomic mass unit is about 1.66 times 10 to the power minus 27 kilograms

kortit.maaritelma: The mass of a bound nucleus is smaller than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons.
The energy needed to break a nucleus into separate nucleons.
kortit.kaava_puhe: E B is delta m times c squared

kortit.maaritelma: The binding energy divided by the number of nucleons in the nucleus describes the stability of the nucleus.
An atomic nucleus changes into another nucleus or other nuclei in an interaction with another particle.
The energy released or taken up in a nuclear reaction is determined by the mass difference between the initial and final states.
kortit.kaava_puhe: Q is the difference m initial minus m final, times c squared

kortit.maaritelma: A heavy atomic nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei and releases energy.
The neutrons released in fission cause new fissions.
Light atomic nuclei combine into a heavier nucleus and can release energy.
The energy of stars is produced when light nuclei combine into larger nuclei.
The energy released in fission is used to produce electrical energy by way of heat.
The smallest amount of fissile material with which a self-sustaining chain reaction is possible.
An unstable atomic nucleus changes by itself into another nucleus and emits radiation as it does so.
The original unstable nucleus of a radioactive decay.
The new atomic nucleus produced in a radioactive decay.
The nucleus emits a helium nucleus that contains two protons and two neutrons.
A neutron of the nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron and an antineutrino are produced.
A proton of the nucleus changes into a neutron, and a positron and a neutrino are produced.
The nucleus captures an electron from the innermost shell of its own atom, so a proton changes into a neutron and a neutrino is produced.
A nucleus in an excited state moves to a lower energy level by emitting a high-energy photon.
Consists of helium nuclei; it ionises strongly but penetrates matter poorly.
Consists of high-speed electrons or positrons.
High-energy electromagnetic radiation with great penetrating power.
A very light, uncharged particle that interacts with matter extremely weakly.
Tells the number of radioactive decays per second.
The unit of activity; one becquerel means one decay per second.
Describes the probability per unit time that a single radioactive nucleus decays.
The time in which the number of radioactive nuclei and the activity of a sample fall to half.
The number of undecayed nuclei decreases exponentially.
kortit.kaava_puhe: N is N zero times e to the power minus lambda t

kortit.maaritelma: The activity of a sample decreases in the same exponential way.
kortit.kaava_puhe: A is A zero times e to the power minus lambda t

kortit.maaritelma: A chain of successive radioactive decays ends in a stable nucleus.
Describes the power carried by radiation per unit area.
The intensity of gamma radiation in matter decreases exponentially as the thickness $d$ of the barrier grows.
kortit.kaava_puhe: I is I zero times e to the power minus mu d

kortit.maaritelma: A constant $\mu$ determined by the material and the energy of the radiation; it tells how strongly the material attenuates the radiation. It is related to the half-value thickness by the equation below.
kortit.kaava_puhe: mu is the natural logarithm of two divided by the half-value thickness

kortit.maaritelma: The thickness of a layer of material that reduces the intensity of radiation to half.
The intensity of the radiation of a point source is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
kortit.kaava_puhe: I is proportional to one divided by r squared

kortit.maaritelma: A photon gives all its energy to an electron of the matter and disappears.

An interaction between a photon and an electron of the matter in which the photon gives part of its energy to the electron and continues in a new direction with less energy; the most important way gamma radiation is attenuated at medium energies.
A photon of high enough energy can change into an electron and a positron near a nucleus.
Radiation whose single particles or photons have enough energy to release electrons from atoms or molecules.
Tells the radiation energy transferred to matter per unit mass.
The unit of absorbed dose.
kortit.kaava_puhe: one gray is one joule per kilogram

kortit.maaritelma: Takes into account, in addition to the absorbed energy, the biological effect of the type of radiation.
The unit of a dose that describes the biological harm of radiation.
Ionising radiation that is constantly present in the environment from natural and artificial sources.
A radioactive gas that moves from the ground into buildings and is the largest source of radiation dose in Finland.
Exposure is reduced by shortening the time, increasing the distance and using suitable shielding.
Ionising radiation can damage cells and DNA and increase the risk of cancer.
Different tissues of the body attenuate X-radiation differently, so an image of the internal structures is formed.
A computer forms a cross-sectional or three-dimensional image of the body from many X-ray images.
Radioactive tracers are used to study the functioning of the body and to treat diseases.
A tracer that emits positrons is used to form an image of the metabolism of the body.
Ionising radiation is aimed at a tumour to damage cancer cells.
The age of an organic sample is estimated from the remaining amount of the isotope carbon-14.
In some detectors a radioactive substance ionises the air, which makes it possible to detect smoke.
A theory that describes the fundamental particles of matter and the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions.
A particle that, according to current knowledge, has no internal structure.
A fundamental particle of matter from which, for example, protons and neutrons are built.
A group of fundamental particles that includes, for example, the electron and the neutrinos.
A particle of a quantum field by which an interaction can be described.
The mediator particle of the strong interaction.
The W and Z bosons mediate the weak interaction.
A particle associated with the Higgs field; its detection supports the model that explains the masses of particles.
The counterpart of a particle, with the same mass but opposite properties, such as electric charge.
When a particle and its antiparticle meet, both can disappear, and all their energy is carried away by, for example, photons.
Keeps quarks together in hadrons and binds protons and neutrons in the atomic nucleus.
Causes, for example, beta decay and changes the type of particles.
Studies the smallest known building blocks of matter and the interactions between them.
Studies the universe as a whole, and its structure, development and contents.
According to the model, the universe developed from a very hot and dense initial state.
A phase of very rapid expansion of the early universe.
In the early universe protons and neutrons formed the first atomic nuclei.
Electrons bound to nuclei to form neutral atoms, after which radiation could travel freely.
An unknown form of matter whose gravitational effect is observed in the motions of galaxies and large structures.
The name for the phenomenon used to explain the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Microwave radiation from the early universe is observed everywhere in space.
The spectrum of distant galaxies shifts to longer wavelengths because of the expansion of the universe.
